Three ideas carry most of the R in this course. R stores things in **objects**,
you do things with **functions**, and the commonest object is a **vector**. Run
the cells, change the numbers, and try things that might not work.

## Objects

`<-` is the assignment arrow. It puts the thing on its right into the name on
its left.

```{webr}
n_screened <- 2400
district   <- "Kolar"

n_screened
district
```

Nothing printed when you assigned. R stored the value silently. Typing the name
on its own line is what prints it.

Change `2400` to a number from your own work and run it again.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
You will see `=` used for assignment in other people's code. It mostly works.
Use `<-` anyway: it is the convention, and `=` means something different inside
a function call, which is exactly where beginners get caught.
:::

## Functions

A function is a verb. It takes **arguments** in brackets, separated by commas,
and gives back a value.

```{webr}
sqrt(144)
round(3.14159, 2)
nchar("epidemiology")
```

`round(3.14159, 2)` passed 2 arguments: the number, and how many decimal
places. Most confusion about R functions is confusion about which argument is
which.

You can name arguments, and then the order stops mattering:

```{webr}
round(x = 3.14159, digits = 2)
round(digits = 2, x = 3.14159)
```

## Vectors

A vector is several values of the same type in a row. `c()` combines them. The
`c` is for *combine*.

```{webr}
# Malaria cases notified in six consecutive months
cases <- c(14, 22, 31, 27, 19, 11)

cases
length(cases)
```

Functions applied to a vector work on every element at once. There is no loop to
write.

```{webr}
cases <- c(14, 22, 31, 27, 19, 11)

sum(cases)
mean(cases)
max(cases)
range(cases)
```

Arithmetic works the same way. This is **vectorisation**, and it is why R code
for data work is usually short.

```{webr}
cases      <- c(14, 22, 31, 27, 19, 11)
population <- c(12000, 12000, 12500, 12500, 13000, 13000)

# cases per 1000 population, month by month
cases / population * 1000
```

Six divisions, one line, no loop.

## Types

A vector holds one type. The 3 you will meet most often:

```{webr}
counts   <- c(14, 22, 31)                       # numeric
district <- c("Kolar", "Tumkur", "Hassan")      # character
exposed  <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)                # logical

class(counts)
class(district)
class(exposed)
```

Mix them and R quietly converts everything to the most forgiving type, usually
character. This is a common source of "why is my column text?".

```{webr}
mixed <- c(14, "Kolar", TRUE)
mixed
class(mixed)
```

Look at what happened: `14` became `"14"`, with quotation marks. You can no
longer take its mean.

## Comparison, and why logicals matter

Comparing a vector gives you a logical vector, one answer per element.

```{webr}
# Ages of 8 participants
age <- c(34, 51, 22, 67, 45, 19, 58, 40)

age >= 45
```

And a logical vector sums as if `TRUE` were 1 and `FALSE` were 0. So `sum()`
counts, and `mean()` gives a proportion.

```{webr}
age <- c(34, 51, 22, 67, 45, 19, 58, 40)

sum(age >= 45)     # how many
mean(age >= 45)    # what proportion
```

That second line is prevalence in miniature: the share of a group who have
something. Primer 6 does it properly.

## Missing values

Real data has holes. R writes a hole as `NA`, and it is contagious on purpose:
the mean of a set of numbers you do not fully know is not knowable.

```{webr}
sbp <- c(128, 142, NA, 136, 151, NA, 119)

mean(sbp)
```

You get `NA`, not an error. R is telling you the answer depends on the 2 values
you do not have.

To average only the ones you do have, say so:

```{webr}
sbp <- c(128, 142, NA, 136, 151, NA, 119)

mean(sbp, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(is.na(sbp))     # how many are missing
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## `na.rm = TRUE` is a decision, not a fix
It changes the question. You asked for the mean of 7 people. You now have the
mean of the 5 you measured.

Sometimes that is fine. Sometimes the 2 missing people are missing *because*
they were the sickest. Then it is not fine. Ask why the values are missing
before you drop them.
:::

## What you should now be able to do

- Store a value in a name with `<-`, and print it by typing the name.
- Call a function with positional or named arguments.
- Build a vector with `c()`, and apply a function to all of it at once.
- Recognise the three common types, and why mixing them turns numbers to text.
- Count and take proportions with `sum()` and `mean()` over a comparison.
- See `NA` for what it is, and decide about it deliberately.
